findings.title: Denial cache takes precedence over fresh grants, extending wrongful denials after permission changes
findings.body: In Check, the permDenialCache is consulted before anything else and short-circuits with Allowed=false. Once a denial is cached (line 154), a user who is subsequently granted the permission (e.g. an admin adds them to a team/role, or a folder permission is created) will still be denied for up to shortCacheTTL (30s), and unlike the allow path there is no DB fallback for denial hits — even a fresh DB query showing the grant is never performed. This asymmetry means the very problem this PR fixes for grants (stale allow/deny after change) now also applies to denials with no re-query escape hatch. Consider falling through to a DB re-check when a denial entry exists but the permission grant may have changed, or at least documenting/acknowledging the up-to-30s denial stickiness, and keying the TTL shorter for denials.

findings.title: Denial cache keyed on raw subject UID while permission cache uses resolved UID, causing duplicate/inconsistent entries
findings.body: The denial cache key is built from checkReq.UserUID, which is the raw identifier from the request subject and may be either a numeric user ID or a UID (GetUserIdentifiers explicitly handles both forms). The permission cache, by contrast, is keyed on the resolved userIdentifiers.UID. The same user queried via 'user:123' vs 'user:<uid>' will produce two independent denial entries, and a denial cached under one form will not be hit when the same user is queried under the other form, defeating the fast-deny path and making behavior inconsistent. Resolve the UID (as getCachedIdentityPermissions already does) before building the denial key.
